papers.title: Burning down the mouse: Effects of wildfire and post-fire reseeding on Sin Nombre virus prevalence in its reservoir host
papers.abstract: Abstract Worldwide, physical habitats and biological communities are being reshaped by wildfire. Such changes have obvious potential to alter pathogen ecology, yet few studies, outside of those focused on ectoparasites, have tested the effects of wildfire on pathogen prevalence in wildlife. Even fewer have focused on the impacts of strategies for post-fire remediation on pathogen circulation. Here, we investigated the effect of wildfire and wildfire mitigation on the prevalence and viral load of Sin Nombre virus (SNV) infection in its reservoir host, the western deer mouse, using a study design of matched burned, unburned, and post-burn reseeded sites in northern New Mexico. In total, we screened 411 individual deer mice for SNV via RT-qPCR and analyzed the effect of wildfire and wildfire mitigation on relative mouse abundance, individual infection probability, site-level prevalence and viral load. Relative abundance was highest at reseeded sites, and model selection indicated that habitat structure – particularly the gradient from closed canopy to open-herbaceous habitat, was consistently associated with increased relative abundance. Similarly, SNV prevalence was significantly higher in reseeded sites than either burned or unburned sites but did not differ in burned versus unburned sites. Viral load did not differ between burn history types, and zero-inflated gamma hurdle models did not identify any strong predictors of viral load. Serendipitously, we were also able to investigate the impacts of an El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) cycle on patterns of infection in a subsample of sites that were studied during and one year after an ENSO year and found that SNV prevalence increased significantly post-ENSO. Both reseeding and ENSO deliver resource pulses that can support increases in mouse density and thereby enhance SNV transmission. The impacts of post-fire management practices on SNV prevalence in its reservoir host that were revealed in this study should be considered when implementing such strategies and when utilizing treated areas. Open research statement To ensure transparency and reproducibility, the authors pledge to place all data and any novel code into Dryad upon acceptance of the manuscript.

Such changes have obvious potential to alter pathogen ecology, yet few studies, outside of those focused on ectoparasites, have tested the effects of wildfire on pathogen prevalence in wildlife. Even fewer have focused on the impacts of strategies for post-fire remediation on pathogen circulation. Here, we investigated the effect of wildfire and wildfire mitigation on the prevalence and viral load of Sin Nombre virus (SNV) infection in its reservoir host, the western deer mouse, using a study design of matched burned, unburned, and post-burn reseeded sites in northern New Mexico. In total, we screened 411 individual deer mice for SNV via RT-qPCR and analyzed the effect of wildfire and wildfire mitigation on relative mouse abundance, individual infection probability, site-level prevalence and viral load. Relative abundance was highest at reseeded sites, and model selection indicated that habitat structure – particularly the gradient from closed canopy to open-herbaceous habitat, was consistently associated with increased relative abundance. Similarly, SNV prevalence was significantly higher in reseeded sites than either burned or unburned sites but did not differ in burned versus unburned sites. Viral load did not differ between burn history types, and zero-inflated gamma hurdle models did not identify any strong predictors of viral load. Serendipitously, we were also able to investigate the impacts of an El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) cycle on patterns of infection in a subsample of sites that were studied during and one year after an ENSO year and found that SNV prevalence increased significantly post-ENSO. Both reseeding and ENSO deliver resource pulses that can support increases in mouse density and thereby enhance SNV transmission. The impacts of post-fire management practices on SNV prevalence in its reservoir host that were revealed in this study should be considered when implementing such strategies and when utilizing treated areas. Open research statement To ensure transparency and reproducibility, the authors pledge to place all data and any novel code into Dryad upon acceptance of the manuscript.

The impacts of post-fire 41 management practices on SNV prevalence in its reservoir host that were revealed in this study 42 should be considered when implementing such strategies and when utilizing treated areas. 43 Introduction 44 Wildfires are increasing in both severity and frequency across the globe, driven by rising 45 temperatures and shifting rainfall patterns (Cunningham et al., 2024; Dennison et al., 2014; 46 Salguero et al., 2020; Westerling et al., 2006). Wildfires can dramatically reshape natural 47 landscapes through reduction of ground litter, loss of canopy cover, and transformation of soil 48 chemistry, among many other effects (Bansal, 2025). Following a wildfire, managers may 49 implement strategies to prevent soil erosion, such as reseeding, replanting, mulching or chemical 50 treatments. These interventions may alleviate some negative effects of wildfire, such as runoff or 51 mudslides, but may exacerbate others, such as alteration of plant communities (Keeley, 2004). 52 These wholesale changes in both burned and remediated landscapes have the potential to alter 53 the transmission of pathogens among wildlife, thereby altering the risk of pathogen spillover to 54 humans. In an increasingly flammable world, it is critical to gain an understanding of the effects 55 of fire on wildlife infection. 56 Albery et al. (2021) have laid out multiple, intersecting mechanisms by which the consequences 57 of wildfire could influence the exposure of wildlife to pathogens. At the nexus of this framework 58 are the impacts of fire on host movement and resource availability. For directly-transmitted 59 pathogens, wildfire may enhance inter-individual contact rates, and therefore transmission, via 60 degradation of habitat complexity, concentration of existing resources, or production of resource 61 pulses that support increases in the host population density. Alternatively, wildfire may reduce 62 contact rates through habitat fragmentation, fire-mediated mortality, or production of resource 63 pulses that disincentivize host foraging movements (Fay et al., 2025; Tonelli et al., 2026). Thus, 64 wildfire may shape infection dynamics through multiple, potentially opposing, mechanisms. 65 Although Albery et al. (2021) did not consider post-fire mitigation, it is clear that some 66 management strategies may also affect host movement and host density. In particular, post-fire 67 reseeding provides a large pulse in resources for granivores that may drive surges in their 68 populations, and the plants that sprout from supplementary seeds may alter vegetation structure 69 and plant community composition. 70 To date, the majority of studies investigating the impact of wildfire on the frequency of wildlife 71 infection have focused on ectoparasites (reviewed in Scasta, 2015) or on proxies of disease risk, 72 such as corticosteroid levels (Hing et al., 2017), immune function, or immune proteomes (Black 73 et al., 2017; Bowen et al., 2015) rather than directly measuring wildfire impacts on pathogen 74 prevalence. Two notable exceptions are work by Ecke et al. (2019) and Furtado et al. (2023). 75 The former showed that wildfire-induced thermal stress may increase host susceptibility to 76 parasitic infection in Tropidurus oreadicus lizards, and the latter demonstrated that reduced 77 habitat complexity correlated with increased Puumala virus (PUUV, Orthohantavirus 78 puumalaense) prevalence in bank voles. 79 In the current study, we investigated the effects of wildfires and post-fire management in 80 northern New Mexico on Sin Nombre virus (SNV, Orthohantavirus sinnombreense) infection of 81 western deer mice (Peromyscus sonoriensis). Western deer mice serve as a major reservoir host 82 of SNV. Increases in SNV prevalence in deer mice are associated with increases in spillover of 83 the virus to humans, in whom it can cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) with a 84 fatality rate of ~35% (Childs et al., 1994; Center for Disease Control, 2024). SNV circulation in 85 deer mice is sensitive to ecological perturbations that alter mouse density, as the virus is 86 transmitted via direct, aggressive contacts, primarily among adult males, that can increase with 87 density (Mills et al., 1997; Pearce-Duvet et al., 2006). In particular, SNV prevalence in deer 88 mouse populations, and subsequent human outbreaks, have been linked to El Niño Southern 89 Oscillation (ENSO) events, which drive increased precipitation throughout the western United 90 States, leading to mast seed production of piñon trees, a food resource pulse that supports 91 increases in deer mouse density (Carver et al., 2015; Parmenter et al., 1993). While ENSO 92 cycles provide a well-established example of how ecological perturbations can alter the SNV 93 system within deer mice, wildfire and post-fire mitigation may act via similar mechanisms. 94 Populations of Peromyscus spp. have generally been shown to increase following both wild and 95 prescribed fires, likely due to release of competition with members of their guild and increased 96 foraging efficiency in the absence of ground litter (reviewed in Jones, 1992; Zwolak et al., 2010). 97 Such increases in host abundance could accelerate SNV transmission and enhance prevalence. 98 Consistent with this paradigm, Mull et al. (2023) reported that more rodents were seropositive 99 for orthohantaviruses in burned prairies in the U.S. compared to clear cut or unmanaged control 100 areas, and Gheler-Costa et al. (2022) found Brazilian Sigmodontinae rodents experienced much 101 faster population growth and were more frequently positive for orthohantaviruses after sugarcane 102 harvest fires than in areas where fire had been suppressed. However, fire effects are unlikely to 103 be universal. Sharp Bowman et al. (2017) found that fires in the Great Basin, USA decreased 104 Peromyscus population sizes, suggesting that severe fires may result in unsuitable habitat and 105 decreased host abundance. Post-fire aerial reseeding may further modify these relationships. By 106 providing an artificial resource pulse, reseeding may act in an analogous fashion to resource 107 pulses associated with ENSO cycles, supporting higher densities of deer mice and elevating SNV 108 prevalence (Figure 1). However, as reseeding also alters habitat composition and vegetation 109 structure, its effects may not be mediated solely by host density. 110 These previous studies of deer mouse and SNV dynamics offer the rationale for the central 111 hypothesis of this study, that changes in habitat structure and resource availability mediated by 112 wildfire and post-fire management will lead to higher SNV prevalence within deer mouse 113 populations via their effects on deer mouse abundance. Our study was conducted in northern 114 New Mexico in the southwest United States, a region that has been ravaged by wildfires during 115 the last decade. We tested several predictions stemming from our central hypothesis, namely: (1) 116 relative abundance of deer mice and prevalence of SNV in deer mice would be higher in sites 117 that had recently burned in a wildfire compared to ecologically-matched, unburned control sites 118 (Figure 1A and 1B), and (2) relative abundance of deer mice and SNV prevalence would be 119 higher in sites that had recently burned in a wildfire and been reseeded post-fire compared to 120 burned sites that had not been reseeded and unburned sites (Figure 1D). Serendipitously, because 121 2023 was an El Niño year, we were also able to test (3) whether prevalence of SNV would 122 increase at a one-year lag following an ENSO event (Figure 1C), as has been demonstrated 123 previously in the desert southwest (Engelthaler et al., 1999; Yates et al., 2002). Additionally, we 124 tested whether two other well recognized patterns in SNV prevalence also held true in our data: 125 (4) SNV prevalence would be higher in adult male than female mice, and higher in adults than 126 juveniles (Douglass et al., 2001; Mills et al., 1997), and (5) SNV prevalence would correlate with 127 degree of wounding (Douglass et al., 2001). Finally, although we had no a priori reason to 128 expect a difference, we nonetheless tested (6) whether SNV viral load in individual mice differed 129 among burn history types. To address our predictions, we live-trapped deer mice over the 130 summers in 2023 and 2024 at areas that had burned with high intensity one or two years 131 previously and were or were not reseeded, as well as at ecologically-matched, unburned control 132 sites. SNV infection of these mice was detected via RT-qPCR of collected lung tissues. 133 134 Figure 1. Predicted effects of wildfire and resource pulses due to reseeding or an ENSO event on 135 vegetation, deer mouse abundance, and SNV prevalence in deer mice. The total number of mice 136 represent the relative abundance of deer mice in a given burn history type; red mice represent 137 SNV positive mice; black mice represent SNV negative mice. A) Independent of ENSO, we 138 predict that unburned sites will remain unchanged in vegetation structure, deer mouse 139 abundance, and SNV prevalence; B) Independent of ENSO, we predict that burned sites will 140 experience substantial vegetation loss, increased mouse abundance and a concomitant increase in 141 SNV prevalence due to wildfire; C) When ENSO occurs, we predict that burned sites will 142 experience a pulse in seed production, which in turn will support even higher levels of deer 143 mouse density than scenario B, and therefore higher SNV prevalence; D) When burned sites are 144 subject to aerial reseeding, we predict that this resource pulse will act similarly to the natural 145 resource pulse triggered by ENSO in scenario C. 146 147 Methods and Materials 148 Ethical Approvals and Permits 149 All procedures on mice were approved by the New Mexico State University Institutional Animal 150 Care and Use Committee (approval number 2404001125) and permission was given by the 151 Jemez and Pecos Las Vegas Ranger districts to trap mice within their respective national forests. 152 Field procedures were conducted following the Animal Care and Use guidelines of the American 153 Society of Mammologists (Sikes and Gannon, 2011). 154 Study Areas 155 This study was conducted in northern New Mexico (NM) (Figure 2A), an area that experiences 156 mild summer temperatures with highs averaging 290C, extreme winter temperatures dipping as 157 low as -340C, and seasonal precipitation occurring during summer monsoons and winter 158 snowstorms (Figure 3). Northern NM has experienced multiple large fires in the last few years, 159 including the two foci of this study, the Cerro Pelado fire and the Hermit’s Peak/Calf Canyon 160 fire. The Cerro Pelado fire, which began in April 2022, seven miles east of the village of Jemez 161 Springs, NM, USA (350 46’ 30” latitude, -1060 35’ 4” longitude), was a mixed severity fire that 162 burned over 45,000 acres (Figure 2B). The Hermit’s Peak fire started as a prescribed burn but 163 was declared a wildfire on April 6, 2022. The Calf Canyon fire started as a pile burn holdover in 164 January and re-emerged in April 2022. The two fires eventually merged into one, becoming the 165 largest and most devastating fire in New Mexico state history. The Hermit’s Peak Calf Canyon 166 complex fire burned over 341,000 acres in the Santa Fe National Forest and surrounding areas 167 near Las Vegas, NM (105°20'19" latitude, 35°48'59" longitude; Figure 2D). 168 To assess the impact of habitat alterations due to fire and post-fire mitigation on relative mouse 169 abundance and SNV prevalence and viral load, mice were live-trapped at 3 sites each in areas 170 affected by the Cerro Pelado or the Hermit’s Peak-Calf Canyon fire, as well as 3 ecologically- 171 matched, unburned control sites for each fire, and 2 sites that had burned and been reseeded, for 172 a total of 14 sites (Figure 2C and 2E). Trapping was initially intended to occur at the Cerro 173 Pelado fire sites in 2023 and the Hermit’s Peak-Calf Canyon fire sites in 2024 (Figure 2F). 174 However, in 2023, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) declared the 175 arrival of an El Niño event during our sampling session (NOAA, 2023). To test the impact of El 176 Niño on SNV prevalence in deer mice, the burned sites in the Cerro Pelado fire were resampled 177 in 2024 (Figure 2F); time restrictions prevented the resampling of the unburned sites. 178 Additionally, trapping was initially intended to occur at three reseeded sites, but extreme rainfall 179 washed out the road to our final reseeded site, making it inaccessible. Instead, we re-sampled the 180 site with the lowest trap success (unburned Site ‘U3’) to attempt to standardize representation 181 across all burn history types. The data from the resampled site was not treated as an independent 182 site, but as a continuation of the previous trapping iteration. 183 184 Figure 2. A) The state of New Mexico in the United States of America with locations of Cerro 185 Pelado fire (left black box) and Hermit’s Peak Calf Canyon (right black box); B) Cerro Pelado 186 fire perimeter; sampling area denoted by red box; C) Locations of burned and unburned sites. 187 Burned sites represented by fire icons, unburned sites denoted by tree icons; D) Hermit’s Peak 188 Calf Canyon fire perimeter; sampling area denoted by red box; E) Locations of burned, 189 unburned, and reseeded sites. Burned sites represented by fire icons, unburned sites represented 190 by tree icons, reseeded sites represented by grass icons; F) Sampling timeline; “CP” stands for 191 Cerro Pelado; “HPCC” stands for Hermit’s Peak Calf Canyon. Map was created with ArcGIS 192 Pro. Icons are from Canva free edition. 193 194 Sampling Sites 195 Burned sites were constrained to areas categorized as high severity soil burn, determined by a 196 post-fire BAER (burned action emergency response) survey conducted by the U.S. Forest 197 Service (NM Fire Info 2022). To select burned sites, first 100 random points were generated 198 within high severity burned areas that were within 500 meters of a road and spaced at least 250 199 meters apart. A buffer of 100 meters was created around the 100 points, and sites for which 200 buffered areas were not completely within a high severity burn were excluded. To select 201 unburned sites, 100 unburned points were randomly generated in areas that mirrored burned sites 202 in terms of elevation and dominant vegetation, after which site selection followed the same 203 protocol as for burned sites, save that unburned sites were also excluded if they experienced any 204 burning after 1980, or if they had any visible burn scars upon visual inspection. Both burned and 205 unburned sites that fit all criteria were assigned a number, and final sites were selected with a 206 random number generator, with each burn type replicated three times, and separate control sites 207 selected…

analysis.background: Wildfire is globally reshaping physical habitats and biological communities, which can alter pathogen ecology. Few studies have examined wildfire effects on pathogen prevalence beyond ectoparasites.
analysis.methods: The authors used a matched design of burned, unburned, and post‑burn reseeded sites in northern New Mexico, screening 411 western deer mice for Sin Nombre virus by RT‑qPCR.
analysis.results: Relative mouse abundance was highest at reseeded sites; SNV prevalence was significantly higher in reseeded sites than in burned or unburned sites, with no difference between burned and unburned; viral load did not differ among burn histories; ENSO was linked to a significant post‑ENSO increase in SNV prevalence.
analysis.contribution: The findings indicate that post‑fire reseeding and ENSO‑driven resource pulses can boost mouse density and SNV transmission, highlighting considerations for fire‑management strategies.
analysis.limitations: Only abstract and partial text are provided; the paper does not report explicit limitations.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Wildfire reshapes habitats worldwide and may affect pathogen ecology, yet few studies go beyond ectoparasites. Methods: Matched burned, unburned, and reseeded sites in northern New Mexico were sampled, with 411 deer mice screened for Sin Nombre virus via RT‑qPCR. Results: Mouse abundance peaked at reseeded sites; SNV prevalence was higher in reseeded versus burned or unburned sites, unchanged between burned and unburned, while viral load showed no burn‑type effect; ENSO was associated with increased prevalence post‑ENSO. papers.title: Temporal trends in critical care burden and outcomes of Andes virus-associated hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome: a national Chilean cohort.
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: Andes virus causes hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), a severe disease found in central and southern parts of Chile and Argentina. Recently a case-outbreak of HCPS was reported on a cruise ship, therefore contemporary data on organ support and outcomes is required. The objective of this study was to assess organ support use and patient outcomes in patients admitted with HCPS. METHODS: We used the Diagnosis-Related Groups (DGR) database to analyse patients admitted in 31 Chilean hospitals between January 1, 2019, and December 31, 2024. They were stratified by the maximal respiratory support received: no respiratory support, non-invasive ventilation (NIV), invasive mechanical ventilation (MV) or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). Hospital length of stay (LOS) and in-hospital mortality were the main outcomes assessed. In-hospital mortality was further analysed by pre-COVID-19 pandemic, pandemic, and post-pandemic periods. RESULTS: A total of 215 patients with HCPS were identified, of whom 69.3% were males and 87% were adults. Of 148 patients who required respiratory support, 14.2% received NIV, 36.5% received MV and 49.3% required ECMO. Hospital LOS was 8 [3-15] days and in-hospital mortality was 20.5%. Case fatality rates were 29.6% for patients receiving MV and 32.9% for those receiving ECMO. The pandemic period was independently associated with higher in-hospital mortality (aOR 2.73 [1.06-7.63]; p = 0.045). CONCLUSION: HCPS caused by Andes virus remains associated with high in-hospital mortality and substantial amounts of respiratory support, particularly MV and ECMO. Moreover, the COVID-19 pandemic was associated with a significant increase in HCPS mortality.

Recently a case-outbreak of HCPS was reported on a cruise ship, therefore contemporary data on organ support and outcomes is required. The objective of this study was to assess organ support use and patient outcomes in patients admitted with HCPS. Methods We used the Diagnosis-Related Groups (DGR) database to analyse patients admitted in 31 Chilean hospitals between January 1, 2019, and December 31, 2024. They were stratified by the maximal respiratory support received: no respiratory support, non-invasive ventilation (NIV), invasive mechanical ventilation (MV) or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). Hospital length of stay (LOS) and in-hospital mortality were the main outcomes assessed. In-hospital mortality was further analysed by pre-COVID-19 pandemic, pandemic, and post-pandemic periods. Results A total of 215 patients with HCPS were identified, of whom 69.3% were males and 87% were adults. Of 148 patients who required respiratory support, 14.2% received NIV, 36.5% received MV and 49.3% required ECMO. Hospital LOS was 8 [3–15] days and in-hospital mortality was 20.5%. Case fatality rates were 29.6% for patients receiving MV and 32.9% for those receiving ECMO. The pandemic period was independently associated with higher in-hospital mortality (aOR 2.73 [1.06–7.63]; p = 0.045). Conclusion HCPS caused by Andes virus remains associated with high in-hospital mortality and substantial amounts of respiratory support, particularly MV and ECMO. Moreover, the COVID-19 pandemic was associated with a significant increase in HCPS mortality. papers.title: DNA and mRNA Vaccines Against Hantaviruses: Antigen Design, Delivery Strategies and Translational Progress
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are members of the Hantaviridae family, which can cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). At present, no specific antiviral treatment is available for hantavirus infection, while licensed hantavirus vaccines are restricted to a limited number of countries in Asia. This review summarizes recent advances in hantavirus DNA and messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines, focusing on antigen design, delivery systems, immunogenicity, safety and translational development. Peer-reviewed studies published primarily within the past 10 years were evaluated together with available hantavirus vaccine trials registered in ClinicalTrials.gov, with emphasis on Hantaan virus (HTNV), Puumala virus (PUUV) and Andes virus (ANDV). DNA vaccine candidates have demonstrated immunogenicity in preclinical and early clinical studies, with an acceptable safety profile. mRNA vaccines represent a newer approach with promising preclinical evidence of humoral and cellular immune responses. However, they have not yet been evaluated clinically. Studies have also reported the potential for varying degrees of cross-protection between hantavirus species, although protection remains limited by antigenic diversity. Overall, current evidence supports further development of nucleic acid-based hantavirus vaccines, particularly multivalent strategies, with emphasis on standardized evaluation and clinical efficacy.

source_records.abstract: Hantaviruses are members of the Hantaviridae family, which can cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). At present, no specific antiviral treatment is available for hantavirus infection, while licensed hantavirus vaccines are restricted to a limited number of countries in Asia. This review summarizes recent advances in hantavirus DNA and messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines, focusing on antigen design, delivery systems, immunogenicity, safety and translational development. Peer-reviewed studies published primarily within the past 10 years were evaluated together with available hantavirus vaccine trials registered in ClinicalTrials.gov, with emphasis on Hantaan virus (HTNV), Puumala virus (PUUV) and Andes virus (ANDV). analysis.background: Hantaviruses cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, and no specific antivirals exist; licensed vaccines are limited to a few Asian countries.
analysis.main_directions: The review summarizes recent DNA and mRNA vaccine designs, delivery platforms, immunogenicity, safety, and translational progress, with emphasis on HTNV, PUUV and ANDV.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause HFRS and HCPS and lack specific antivirals, with licensed vaccines restricted to a few Asian nations. Main directions: The review covers recent DNA and mRNA vaccine designs, delivery methods, immunogenicity, safety, and translational progress, focusing on HTNV, PUUV and ANDV. Current state: DNA vaccines are immunogenic and safe in early studies; mRNA vaccines elicit strong immune responses preclinically but have no clinical data. Gaps: Clinical evaluation of mRNA vaccines is absent and cross‑protection is limited by antigenic diversity. Future research: Prioritize multivalent nucleic‑acid vaccines, standardized efficacy testing, and clinical trials to establish safety and protection.

papers.title_zh: DNA和mRNA疫苗针对汉坦病毒es:抗原设计、递送策略与转化进展

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒es 引起 肾综合征出血热 和 汉坦病毒心肺综合征,且暂无特异性抗病毒药物;获批疫苗仅限于少数亚洲国家。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 该综述概述了近期DNA和mRNA疫苗的设计、递送平台、免疫原性、安全性以及转化进展,重点关注HTNV、PUUV和ANDV。
analysis_zh.current_state: DNA疫苗在临床前和早期临床研究中已显示免疫原性和可接受的安全性,而mRNA疫苗在临床前模型中表现出强烈的体液和细胞免疫应答,但尚缺乏临床评估。
analysis_zh.gaps: mRNA候选疫苗尚未在人体中进行测试,且由于抗原多样性,汉坦病毒物种之间的交叉保护有限。
analysis_zh.future_research: 开发多价核酸疫苗,采用标准化的效力评估,并开展临床试验以确认安全性和保护效力。

papers.summary_zh: 背景：汉坦病毒es 引起 肾综合征出血热 和 汉坦病毒心肺综合征,且暂无特异性抗病毒药物;获批疫苗仅限于少数亚洲国家。 主要方向：该综述概述了近期DNA和mRNA疫苗的设计、递送平台、免疫原性、安全性以及转化进展,重点关注HTNV、PUUV和ANDV。 研究现状：DNA疫苗在临床前和早期临床研究中已显示免疫原性和可接受的安全性,而mRNA疫苗在临床前模型中表现出强烈的体液和细胞免疫应答,但尚缺乏临床评估。 不足：mRNA候选疫苗尚未在人体中进行测试,且由于抗原多样性,汉坦病毒物种之间的交叉保护有限。 后续研究：开发多价核酸疫苗,采用标准化的效力评估,并开展临床试验以确认安全性和保护效力。

papers.title: Orthohantaviruses in Wastewater: Transmission Risks and Opportunities for Early Warning
papers.abstract: Abstract The recent outbreak of Andes virus, a rodentborne orthohantavirus, on the cruise ship MV Hondius has received significant media attention, with suggested gaps in response giving rise to concerns about preparedness for the spread of rare zoonotic disease. Early warning of infection spread, such as that obtained through wastewater surveillance (WS), could greatly benefit public health management and interventions for orthohantavirus infections, particularly in regions with limited clinical surveillance. Given the similarities between orthohantaviruses and other enveloped RNA viruses successfully monitored through WS, many of the principles developed by the global WS community over the past several years may be transferable and rapidly implementable for orthohantavirus surveillance. With a specific focus on Andes virus, Sin Nombre virus, Hantaan virus, and Puumala virus, we present key features of orthohantaviruses relevant to advancing quantification efforts and interpreting wastewater data. We summarize the current state of knowledge related to orthohantavirus shedding in excretions relevant to wastewater, highlight case studies documenting orthohantaviruses in wastewater, and discuss promising approaches for implementing WS. Because orthohantaviruses are shed in rodent excretions and the habitats of these rodents are often associated with sanitation systems, the interpretation of orthohantavirus genetic markers in wastewater samples requires careful consideration. Furthermore, based on findings from previous WS studies and current knowledge regarding the environmental persistence of enveloped viruses similar to ANDV, the risk of transmission through wastewater is likely low but not negligible. Key gaps in our understanding include orthohantavirus survival in environmental matrices (particularly wastewater and aerosols) as well as the development and validation of quantitative assays in environmental contexts, which are required for robust WS programs. Further, deployment of assays targeting orthohantaviruses in WS at sentinel sites, such as airports, hospitals, or cruise ships, would be helpful to understand outbreak boundaries. Thoughtful application of orthohantavirus WS, in coordination with public health agencies and existing surveillance and containment efforts, could not only help prevent disease spread but also serve as an important case study for the rapid translation of WS in response to an emerging disease outbreak.

papers.title: Andes Virus: From Transmission Dynamics to Pandemic Potential.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Andes virus (ANDV) has recently emerged as a significant public health concern following a multi‐country outbreak aboard the MV Hondius cruise ship in April 2026, with 13 identified cases and three deaths among passengers and crew. Methods We reviewed available literature from PubMed and Google Scholar databases and searched international health agencies, including the World Health Organisation and national public health authorities, for current outbreak information and up‐to‐date epidemiological data. Results ANDV is a zoonotic orthohantavirus endemic in southern Chile and Argentina, with Oligoryzomys longicaudatus as its principal reservoir. Approximately 300 cases of hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome occur annually in the Americas. The virus causes severe disease through endothelial dysfunction and vascular leakage, resulting in rapidly progressive pulmonary edema and shock. Human‐to‐human transmission is characteristic of ANDV and occurs through respiratory and salivary routes during prolonged close contact. Clinical presentation includes nonspecific prodromal symptoms followed by rapid cardiopulmonary deterioration. Diagnosis relies on serological assays and RT‐qPCR. Management is predominantly supportive, emphasising hemodynamic monitoring and early consideration of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in severe cases. Conclusions Despite ANDV's severity and high mortality, its epidemic potential seems to be low. However, the recent outbreak underscores the importance of international surveillance coordination and rapid diagnostic capabilities for emerging zoonotic infections.

analysis.background: The review was prompted by a multi‑country Andes virus outbreak aboard the MV Hondius cruise ship in April 2026, which resulted in 13 cases and three deaths (A1).
analysis.main_directions: It surveys literature on ANDV ecology, reservoir species, human‑to‑human respiratory/salivary transmission, endothelial‑mediated pathogenesis, clinical management, and the need for coordinated surveillance (A2, A5, A6, A9).
analysis.current_state: ANDV is an orthohantavirus endemic to southern Chile and Argentina, with Oligoryzomys longicaudatus as the main reservoir; ~300 hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome cases occur annually in the Americas, and disease results from endothelial dysfunction causing pulmonary edema, with documented human‑to‑human spread during close contact (A3, A4, A5, A6).
analysis.gaps: The true pandemic potential remains uncertain despite low estimated risk, and data on transmission dynamics, asymptomatic infection, and effective therapeutics are limited, highlighting fragmented surveillance (A10, A11).
analysis.future_research: Future work should strengthen international surveillance and rapid diagnostics, clarify transmission pathways and viral genetics, and evaluate targeted antivirals or immunotherapies in clinical trials (A11).

analysis.summary_en: Background: The review was prompted by a multi‑country Andes virus outbreak aboard a cruise ship in April 2026 with 13 cases and three deaths (A1). Main directions: It surveys literature on ANDV ecology, reservoir, human‑to‑human transmission, endothelial pathogenesis, clinical management, and surveillance needs (A2, A5, A6, A9). Current state: ANDV is endemic to southern Chile/Argentina, uses Oligoryzomys longicaudatus as reservoir, causes ~300 annual hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome cases in the Americas, and leads to severe pulmonary edema via endothelial dysfunction, with documented human‑to‑human spread (A3, A4, A5, A6). Gaps: Pandemic potential is uncertain, data on transmission, asymptomatic infection, and therapeutics are limited, and surveillance is fragmented (A10, A11). Future research: Strengthen global surveillance, improve rapid diagnostics, study transmission and viral genetics, and test antivirals or immunotherapies (A11).

papers.title_zh: 安第斯病毒:从传播动力学到大流行潜力。

analysis_zh.background: 该综述是因2026年4月在MV Hondius邮轮上发生的跨国 安第斯病毒 疫情而启动的,导致13例感染和3例死亡 (A1)。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本文综述了安第斯病毒的生态学、宿主物种、人际呼吸道/唾液传播、内皮介导的发病机制、临床管理以及协同监测的需求 (A2, A5, A6, A9)。
analysis_zh.current_state: 安第斯病毒是一种 正汉坦病毒 病毒,主要分布于智利南部和阿根廷,以 Oligoryzomys longicaudatus 为主要宿主;美洲每年约有 ~300 汉坦病毒心肺综合征 病例,疾病由内皮功能障碍导致肺水肿,在密切接触中已记录到人际传播 (A3, A4, A5, A6)。

analysis_zh.future_research: 未来工作应加强国际监测和快速诊断,阐明传播途径和病毒基因组,并在临床试验中评估针对性的抗病毒药物或免疫疗法 (A11)。

papers.title: Hantavirus outbreak on a cruise ship: Public health challenges.
papers.abstract: •A rare hantavirus outbreak on MV Hondius in May 2026 caused 8 cases and 3 deaths.•Cruise ship confined spaces and HVAC systems facilitated aerosol transmission.•Jurisdictional disputes delayed critical medical evacuations.•Lack of isolation and diagnostics exposed cruise ship medical vulnerabilities.•Pathogen research and robust maritime emergency protocols are needed.

analysis.background: A rare hantavirus outbreak occurred on the cruise ship MV Hondius in May 2026, raising concerns about aerosol transmission in confined maritime settings.
analysis.methods: Not reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.results: The outbreak involved 8 cases and 3 deaths; aerosol spread was facilitated by the ship’s HVAC system, and jurisdictional disputes delayed medical evacuations, exposing gaps in isolation and diagnostic capacity.
analysis.contribution: The authors call for targeted pathogen research and the development of robust maritime emergency protocols to strengthen public‑health preparedness on cruise vessels.
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract is provided; detailed methods, sample characteristics, and comprehensive epidemiologic data are not reported.
